extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career fiction writers (including indie authors and short-fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on common scams, business mistakes, and community-fit problems writers encounter while building a publishing career, with specific tips for evaluating agents, services, critique groups, and indie publishing partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suspicious when you must pay to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Money flows toward the author; be wary of anyone asking you to pay (e.g., reading fees) in order to be considered for representation or publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone asks for payment (example: a $50 reading fee from an 'agent'), stop and carefully consider whether they're legitimate. Small losses can still feel humiliating; research before sending money. The general adage presented: whenever you're writing a check to someone, stop and decide if this is someone you should be sending money to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trusted watchdog resources and peer research
rubrics_metrics.description: Before engaging with agents, editors, presses, or services, consult watchdog sites and ask other writers about their experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources named: Writer Beware (recommended homework), Predators & Editors (historical example). Talk to other writers and check community threads/forums to see if a person or company has a reputation. Doing this research helps distinguish legitimate opportunities from predatory or incompetent ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate agent legitimacy by client publication record
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate agent should have recent, discoverable authors and books; you should be able to find new books represented by that agent in bookstores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent has not had releases in the last five years or you cannot find authors they represent who are publishing with your target publishers, that agent is likely not a good candidate. Use presence of recent clients and visible book releases as a key signal of an agent's activity and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between scams and incompetence
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all problematic offers are deliberate scams—some people are simply inexperienced or unqualified; both situations can harm your career but require different responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency charging reading fees might be a scam or might be an inexperienced person trying to monetize in the wrong way. Either way, they likely cannot further your career. Research and verification are needed to determine intent, but the practical outcome (avoid or require heavy vetting) is similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize legitimate paid services and conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying for certain services (conferences, freelance editors, legitimate indie-publishing expenses) can be appropriate—payment alone is not proof of a scam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As indie publishing became legitimate, many worthwhile services and conferences charge fees. Learn to distinguish legitimate vendors from predators: look for track records, references, and community recommendations before paying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vanity-publishing and kickback loops
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of cycles where you pay for editing/publishing services that funnel you into publishers/editors who give kickbacks, trapping you in ongoing payments without genuine distribution or career advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The described scam loop: pay for editing → get recommended to a publisher → publisher recommends another paid editor → kickbacks occur and the author keeps paying. Learn the difference between vanity publishing and honest indie publishing; use watchdog resources to spot these loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose critique groups by fit and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what you need from each group (support, critique, accountability) and join multiple groups if necessary; don't expect one group to serve all functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: supportive groups for morale, critique groups for professional feedback, accountabilibuddy pairs for productivity. Misidentifying a group's purpose or adopting a group's mindset that doesn't match your goals can stall your career. Periodically take stock of whether a group's output aligns with your objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distinct readers for different feedback roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment alpha/beta readers and other readers by the role you need them to play—some provide tough, useful critique; others provide encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sending work for feedback, pick readers who will give the kind of response you need: meaningful editorial critique vs. morale-boosting positivity. Managing these roles prevents confusing or unhelpful feedback and supports both craft development and emotional resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt separate 'writer' and 'business' personas
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat your creative self and your business self as distinct roles so you can make clear decisions about submissions, hiring, and marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advice: sometimes you must be the writer (focus on creating) and sometimes the businessperson (decide where to submit, whom to hire, manage finances). Consciously switching perspectives helps avoid naive business decisions and emotional reactions when negotiating services or publishing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet service providers with work samples and business evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When hiring editors, cover artists, developers, or other vendors, require demonstrable past work and evidence they understand your business needs (e.g., portfolios, app examples, business plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard's example: when seeking an app developer, they required applicants to show apps they'd made and present a business plan for how they'd make money with the project. Only those who demonstrated business understanding were hired. Apply similar thresholds to copyeditors, designers, and marketers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set thresholds for partnerships to avoid wasting resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish minimum criteria for working with partners (experience, tangible deliverables, clear plans) so you do not 'hemorrhage money and time'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack experience in hiring or negotiating, set simple, objective thresholds (examples: documented portfolio, recent client successes, clear proposal/business plan) before committing funds. This screening filters out vendors who are inexperienced or who treat authors as marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful that community mindset can shape your writing career
rubrics_metrics.description: The collective attitudes and goals of a group can influence your priorities and methods—ensure you are intentionally choosing communities that support your career orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you aim to publish aggressively, a casual supportive group may be a poor fit and could slow your progress by shaping your expectations. Conversely, if you write for joy, a supportive group is appropriate. Know your goals and select communities that reinforce (not derail) them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer recommendations to validate unknown opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacted by unfamiliar agents or editors, ask peers if they've heard of them or had experience; community signals can quickly reveal red flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erin recommends leveraging the strong short-fiction community to vet contacts. Asking 'Have you heard of this agent/editor?' can surface reputation issues before you engage or pay for services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have at least one accountability partner
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an 'accountabilibuddy'—a partner who helps you with writing discipline and progress tracking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts emphasize everyone should have at least one accountabilibuddy. This role is distinct from critique or support groups and is focused on productivity and consistent work.
